# The Cartography of Wonder

There is a particular kind of silence that settles over a room when someone is truly paying attention—not to the words being spoken, but to the spaces between them. It is the silence of leaning forward, of breath held just a fraction longer, of the heart doing its quiet work behind the ribs. I have been thinking about attention lately, and about what it means to live in a world that has engineered its own distraction.

We live, most of us, in a state of constant partial presence. We are at our desks but thinking about dinner. We are at dinner but checking our phones. We are with our children but mentally composing an email. We are in our emails but wishing we were with our children. This is not a moral failing, exactly—it is the ambient condition of being human in the twenty-first century, the air we breathe without noticing. And yet, somewhere beneath this fractured way of living, there persists a longing for something whole. A longing for unbroken attention. A longing, I have come to believe, for wonder.

Wonder is a word that has grown soft in our mouths, worn smooth by overuse in self-help contexts and TED talks. We speak of "wonder" the way we speak of "wellness"—as a destination one can reach through correct practice, a state of being available for purchase at the right retreat center. But the wonder I mean is not a destination. It is not even, strictly, a state. It is more like a posture, a way of tilting oneself toward the world such that the world becomes visible again. Children are good at this. Adults must relearn it, often painfully, often late.

I remember being seven years old and standing at the edge of a parking lot in suburban New Jersey, watching a line of ants dismantle a dead beetle. I was transfixed—not by the gore of it, which I do not recall, but by the sheer industry of it, the way the ants moved as if choreographed by some invisible conductor, the way they solved a problem too large for any one of them through a logic I could not yet name. I crouched there for what felt like hours. My mother eventually called me, twice, perhaps three times, her voice moving from patient to impatient to concerned. I could not explain what I was looking at. I did not have the words. I only knew that there was something happening that I did not understand, and that not understanding it felt less like ignorance and more like a gift.

That is wonder. It is the experience of standing at the edge of a system too large to comprehend, and finding that the incomprehension itself is a kind of nourishment. It is what happens when we stop trying to make the world fit into our categories and instead let it remain, briefly, uncategorized. We are so eager, as we grow older, to label, to file, to know. We mistake knowing for intimacy. But intimacy, I think, is the opposite of knowing. Intimacy is what happens when we allow something to remain strange to us, when we resist the reflexive urge to convert mystery into fact.

Consider, for a moment, the ordinary miracle of breathing. Air enters the body through the nose or mouth, is warmed and filtered, travels down the trachea, and arrives at the lungs, where it passes through membranes so thin that oxygen molecules slip directly into the bloodstream. Hemoglobin in the red blood cells binds to the oxygen, and these cells—each one smaller than a grain of sand—are pumped by the heart through an estimated sixty thousand miles of blood vessels, delivering their cargo to every cell in the body. The cells use the oxygen to convert glucose into ATP, the energy currency of life, producing carbon dioxide as waste, which then reverses the journey, is exhaled, and disperses into the atmosphere, where it is taken up by plants, which use it, in concert with water and sunlight, to produce more glucose. The whole transaction—the breathing in, the breathing out, the cycling of carbon and oxygen across the porous boundary between animal and atmosphere—has been going on, in one form or another, for billions of years. You are participating in it right now, without your permission, without your awareness, without your gratitude. And this is just breathing. This is just one of the ten thousand processes that must occur, every moment, for you to remain alive for one more second.

I do not know how to hold this knowledge without being undone by it. And yet, I do not hold it at all, most of the time. I hold my phone instead. I hold my opinions instead. I hold my schedule instead. The miracle is happening, and I am looking at a screen.

This is not a sermon against technology. I am typing these words into a machine that is, itself, a kind of miracle—a coordinated dance of transistors and electrons and photons through glass, all orchestrated by a web of human cooperation so vast and intricate that no single mind could map it. I am not against the machine. I am against the forgetting. I am against the way the machine, in solving so many of our problems of access, has subtly reoriented our attention toward the small, the urgent, the frictionless, and away from the slow, the large, the difficult—the things that cannot be swiped.

A few months ago, I went for a walk in the woods behind my house. I had not been there in a long time. The path, which I had walked many times as a younger person, had become overgrown in places, and there were fallen trees across it that required climbing over or ducking under. I was annoyed at first, in the way one is annoyed when the world fails to cooperate with one's expectations. I had wanted a walk, not an obstacle course. But then, somewhere past the third fallen tree, I gave up on the path entirely. I let my feet find their own way. I let my eyes unfocus from the trail ahead and instead take in the periphery—the way the light fell through the canopy in pale columns, the way the moss on a rock glowed almost iridescent in the wet air, the way a small mushroom pushed up through a bed of decaying leaves as if it had somewhere to be.

I stood there for a long time. I do not know how long. Long enough that the light changed, long enough that the temperature dropped a degree or two, long enough that I forgot, briefly, that I was a person with a job and an inbox and a sense of self that required maintenance. I was just a thing in the woods, breathing, looking, being breathed and looked in return. There is a word for this in Japanese—*komorebi*—the dappled light that filters through the leaves. There is a word for this in many languages, I suspect, because the experience itself is not rare. It is only rare that we make room for it.

I have been thinking about the architecture of attention, the way it is shaped by the spaces we inhabit. A room with bare walls invites a different kind of looking than a room with intricate wallpaper. A walk in a place with no signage invites a different kind of attention than a walk through a city with arrows pointing everywhere. There is, I think, a kind of attention that is only possible in the absence of cues. When the world is not telling us where to look, we are free to discover what we notice on our own. And what we notice on our own, in my experience, is almost always more interesting than what we are told to notice.

This is why I am suspicious of curation. Not the kind that helps a museum display its collection, but the kind that has become ambient in our digital lives—the algorithmic curation of our news, our feeds, our entertainment. The algorithms are, in their way, very smart. They learn what we like and give us more of it. But what we like is not always what we need, and what we need is not always what catches our attention. The algorithms optimize for engagement, which is a kind of attention, but it is attention of a thin, hungry, never-satisfied sort. It is the attention of a slot machine, not the attention of a forest.

I am not the first person to notice this. A long line of thinkers—Simone Weil, William James, the desert fathers, the Buddha, the poet Mary Oliver—have all, in their own languages, pointed toward the same truth: that the quality of our attention is the quality of our lives. That to learn to pay attention is, in some sense, the whole project of being human. Mary Oliver, in her poem "The Summer Day," ends with the famous question: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" It is a question, she implies, that can only be properly asked by someone who has first learned to notice that they are alive.

And yet, I do not want to romanticize the difficulty of attention. For some people, sustained attention is not merely a discipline but a survival skill, hard-won against conditions that make focus nearly impossible. For others, the very recommendation to "just be present" can feel like a kind of violence—a privileged instruction that assumes a baseline of safety and quiet that not everyone has. The woods behind my house are not the same woods that everyone can access. The dappled light is not available in the same way to someone working two jobs, or caring for an ill parent, or living in a place where stepping outside is a risk rather than a respite. Wonder is not equally distributed. And pretending that it is, or that attention is simply a matter of choosing it, is a kind of blindness that betrays the very project of clear seeing.

What I can say is that there is something in the human being that, when given even a small opening, reaches toward wonder. It is the same impulse that makes a child press her face against a window to watch the snow. It is the same impulse that makes a tired commuter look up, for just a moment, at a sky so pink it looks like a mistake. It is, perhaps, the deepest of our instincts—animal, pre-verbal, older than language—that the world is more than what we have made of it. The miracle is that this impulse survives at all, given what we have done to silence it. The miracle is that it waits for us, patient as the moss on the rock, ready to glow the moment we turn our eyes toward it.

I think I would like to live a life shaped by that turning. Not perfectly, not heroically, but in the small ways—putting down the phone when the sky is doing something interesting, choosing to be bored sometimes, letting the walk take longer than it needs to, asking the question a moment longer before reaching for the answer. I think I would like to believe that the world is still, despite everything, a place worth the full weight of my attention. And I think that, in the moments when I manage it—when I really manage it, even for a breath, even for a second—there is a kind of joy that does not require a single thing to be added to my life. The joy is that I am in it. The joy is that the breathing is happening. The joy is that the ants are still dismantling their beetles, and the mushrooms are still pushing up, and the light is still falling through the leaves, and I, for once, have not looked away.

That, I think, is enough. That is more than enough. That is everything.
